evidence: M-O s.v. minister, secretary, head of governmental ministry
terms.comment: Classically an attendant, servant or helper, and an under-official (Lewis & Short); in Neo-Latin a minister of state (Morgan–Owens), as in Traupman’s minister prīmārius, prime minister. Rome had no ministers: public business was shared among magistrates elected for a year, and under the emperors among the emperor’s prefects and freedmen.

terms.gloss: a minister, a secretary of state
evidence: M-O s.v. minister, secretary, head of governmental ministry
terms.comment: Classically an assistant or helper (Lewis & Short). Traupman’s word for the American secretaries of state, of the treasury and of the interior; Levi–Bini (p. 41) have rēgiī administrī, the king’s ministers.

terms.grammar: noun phrase: minister with the adjective pūblicus

phrases.english: a foreign minister (Traupman: the secretary of state)

sources: Lewis & Short: minister · Lewis & Short: administer · Lewis & Short: publicus
